results.summary: This design implements a power supply sequencer that can sequentially enable and disable multiple output channels with configurable delays. It uses counters and registers to manage the state of channel activations, with delay inputs setting the counter threshold. The channels can be enabled sequentially starting from channel 0 by asserting the enable pin, and disabled sequentially starting from channel 7 by deasserting it. No external hardware is strictly required, but it is useful for circuits needing sequenced power supplies.

This is a simple UART transmitter module designed to send data serially at a baud rate of 115200. Data is provided in 8-bit parallel format on the input pins, and transmission is initiated by asserting the 'tx_send' pin. The module outputs the serial data on the 'TX' pin and indicates its busy status on the 'tx_busy' pin. No external hardware is specified for testing, but it is intended for serial communication.

This project implements a Pulse Width Modulator (PWM) using Verilog, designed to regulate the power delivered to a device. The duty cycle of the PWM output is controlled by an 8-bit input. The description states it is essential in electronics for energy regulation and adheres to system requirements. Testing is suggested using a Xilinx Basys 3 FPGA.

This design generates a Pulse Width Modulated (PWM) waveform with a duty cycle controlled by a 7-bit input. An internal counter compares against the duty cycle value to determine the output state, allowing for adjustable ON times. To test, a clock signal must be provided, and the duty cycle input adjusted to observe the resulting PWM waveform on an oscilloscope or logic analyzer. An oscilloscope or logic analyzer is recommended as external hardware.

This project plays the Super Mario tune using differential PWM modulation on a piezo speaker. It converts RTTL ringtone data into Verilog using Python. To test, a 100kHz clock is provided on one input, and a brief reset pulse is applied. The Super Mario tune will then play through a piezo speaker connected across two output pins. The required external hardware is a piezo speaker connected to the specified output pins.

This is a Verilog implementation of the AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, capable of producing three square wave tones, a noise generator, and an envelope generator. It replicates the behavior of the classic chip, offering digital outputs for audio via DAC or PWM, and includes a test suite for validation. The design requires external hardware such as a DAC or an RC filter with an amplifier to produce audible sound. Silicon test reports indicate successful operation, producing chiptunes when driven correctly.

This design is a digital PWM generator with selectable resolution, dyadic modulation, and dithering capabilities. It supports 5 to 9 bits of resolution and offers multiple modes including Normal PWM, Dyadic, and three Dithering versions, controllable via a configuration interface. The design produces complementary high- and low-side outputs with dead-time and a sync clock. Testing involves initial reset behavior as an 8-bit PWM, followed by configuration of specific features, and can be verified with the provided cocotb testbench.

This project implements a Spiking Neural Network (SNN) that learns through Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP) and rewards. The network consists of one layer of two neuron loops, which are used to construct an 8-layer SNN. Weights are loaded from memory, and testing involves inputting 32 weights in 4-bit format with a 3-bit layer address and 1-bit node address, followed by inputting two values to execute the network. The specific external hardware requirements are not detailed beyond the input pin functions.

This project implements an AXI-Stream Matrix Vector Multiplier with a UART interface for communication. The design is intended for digital signal processing tasks involving matrix-vector multiplication. Further documentation and testing details are available on the project's GitHub repository. An external USB-FTDI interface is required for UART communication during testing.

Basic8 is a minimal 8-bit CPU featuring 8 general-purpose registers (with r0 hardwired to 0), an 8-bit program counter, and a 16-bit instruction format. It supports ALU operations, immediate operations, and branch/jump instructions. Instructions are loaded in two cycles via the input pins, and the program counter is output externally, allowing an external ROM to feed instructions. Testing requires connecting an external ROM and following a specific sequence of input pin manipulations.
